## The Dehn Function

Let \(G=\langle S\mid R\rangle\) be a finitely presented group. Write \(F(S)\) for the free group on \(S\), and let \(\pi:F(S)\to G\) be the quotient map, so that \(G\cong F(S)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\), where \(\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\) is the normal closure of \(R\) in \(F(S)\).

### Van Kampen diagrams and area

Fix a word \(w\) in the generators \(S\cup S^{-1}\) with \(\pi(w)=1\in G\), i.e. \(w\in\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\). A **van Kampen diagram** \(D\) for \(w\) over the presentation \(\langle S\mid R\rangle\) is a finite, connected, simply connected, planar 2-dimensional CW-complex together with a labeling of each oriented edge by a letter of \(S\cup S^{-1}\) (with orientation reversal inverting the label), such that:

1. Reading the labels around the boundary of each 2-cell (face), following the orientation, gives a word that is a cyclic conjugate of an element of \(R\cup R^{-1}\cup\{1\}\).
2. Reading the labels around the boundary of the whole diagram (with the induced outer orientation) gives the word \(w\) (up to free reduction / insertion of trivial subwords, depending on the convention).

The **area** of the diagram \(D\), denoted \(\operatorname{Area}(D)\), is the number of 2-cells (faces) it contains. Equivalently, it counts how many relator-tiles are glued together to fill the loop labelled by \(w\).

The **area of the word** \(w\) is then

\[
\operatorname{Area}(w)\;=\;\min\bigl\{\operatorname{Area}(D)\;:\;D\text{ is a van Kampen diagram for }w\bigr\}.
\]

This minimum is finite because \(w\in\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\), so \(w\) can be expressed as a product of conjugates of elements of \(R\cup R^{-1}\); each such conjugate corresponds to one 2-cell, and the diagram is the geometric realization of that expression. Taking the minimum corresponds to choosing the most efficient filling.

### Definition of the Dehn function

The **Dehn function** of \(G\) (with respect to the finite presentation \(\langle S\mid R\rangle\)) is

\[
\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\;=\;\max\bigl\{\,\operatorname{Area}(w)\;:\;w\text{ a word over }S\cup S^{-1},\;\ell(w)\le n,\;\pi(w)=1\,\bigr\},
\]

where \(\ell(w)\) is the free length of \(w\) (number of letters). In words: among all words of length at most \(n\) that represent the identity in \(G\), take the one that is hardest to fill, and record the area of its most efficient filling. That worst-case area is \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\).

### How it measures the difficulty of the word problem

The word problem for \(G\) asks: given a word \(w\) of length \(\le n\), decide whether \(\pi(w)=1\). A positive certificate that \(\pi(w)=1\) is precisely a van Kampen diagram for \(w\); its area is the size of that certificate. Hence:

- \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\) is the **minimal worst-case size of a certificate** needed to prove that a word of length \(\le n\) is trivial.
- The time/space complexity of any "filling-based" algorithm for the word problem is bounded below by the growth rate of \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}\). Concretely, a naive Dehn-reduction / diagram-search algorithm runs in time polynomial in \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\) (one must enumerate diagrams of area up to \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\)), so the asymptotic growth of the Dehn function controls the algorithmic difficulty:
  - \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\preceq n\) (linear) — e.g. hyperbolic groups — the word problem is solvable in linear time.
  - \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\preceq n^{2}\) — automatic groups, including virtually abelian and many Coxeter groups.
  - \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}(n)\preceq n^{\alpha}\) for various \(\alpha\), or \(\exp(n)\), or worse — correspondingly harder word problems.
  - \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}\) grows faster than every recursive function exactly when the word problem is **unsolvable** for that finitely presented group.

Here \(\preceq\) denotes the usual preorder: \(f\preceq g\) iff \(f(n)\le C\,g(Cn)+C\) for some constant \(C\) and all large \(n\). The Dehn function is well-defined up to this equivalence because changing the finite presentation only changes \(\operatorname{Dehn}_{G}\) by a \(\preceq\)-equivalence (Tietze transformations modify area by at most a linear-in-\(n\) multiplicative factor and a polynomial distortion of length).

### Summary of the mechanism

A word \(w\) of length \(\le n\) representing the identity is a closed loop in the Cayley 2-complex of \(\langle S\mid R\rangle\). Reducing \(w\) to the identity means contracting this loop to a point inside the complex. Each 2-cell (each relator) is a "move" that fills in a piece of the loop. The **area** is the number of such moves needed in the most economical filling. The Dehn function takes the maximum such area over all loops of perimeter \(\le n\), and thereby quantifies, as a function of input length, how hard it is to certify triviality — i.e. how hard the word problem is.

### PROOF COMPLETE
